description:
Wesam Saad continues the discussion of spiritual gifts by examining teaching, wisdom, exhortation and mercy. Teaching involves helping others understand Scripture as its author intended, rather than simply possessing impressive knowledge. He distinguishes that work from preaching, which addresses the mind while also engaging the affections and calling for a response. Drawing on James 3:1, he urges teachers to prepare carefully, repent of sin and depend on God. The discussion of wisdom challenges self-preservation as the controlling measure of a good decision. Stephen’s witness in Acts 6 provides the example, while Wesam explicitly rejects deliberately seeking danger to prove one’s spirituality.

Exhortation is presented as coming alongside someone with comfort, correction and encouragement towards growth. Mercy involves sharing another person’s sorrow or joy with deep compassion. Although every believer is called to these qualities, Wesam describes particular giftedness as a distinctive capacity to build others up. He then returns to love, character and the church’s responsibility when a member wants to serve. Refusing a platform can be appropriate while character and faithful service are tested; favouritism or controlling obstruction is a different matter. Listeners are encouraged to begin serving on a smaller scale, accept the body’s discernment and pursue lasting edification rather than attention.

questions.question: What distinguishes the gift of teaching from knowledge alone?
questions.answer: Wesam says a teacher must help listeners understand Scripture accurately and coherently as the author intended. A large store of knowledge or an impressive presentation is insufficient if the hearers cannot understand. He distinguishes this from preaching, which includes instruction but also engages the affections and calls the will to respond.

questions.question: Why does a teacher’s character matter alongside their ability?
questions.answer: Wesam connects gifted teaching with dependence on the Holy Spirit, personal attention to Scripture, repentance and careful preparation. He appeals to James 3:1 concerning teachers’ greater accountability. Ability to explain a passage therefore does not remove the need for a life that is being shaped by the truth taught.

questions.question: How does Stephen’s example challenge a self-protective understanding of wisdom?
questions.answer: Wesam points to Acts 6:10, where Stephen’s opponents cannot withstand his wisdom and the Spirit with which he speaks. Stephen’s eventual death does not, in his account, prove that his witness was foolish. He contrasts preserving oneself at any cost with seeking God’s glory in the opportunity given, while expressly rejecting deliberately seeking danger.

questions.question: Does exhortation mean only making someone feel better?
questions.answer: Wesam describes coming alongside a person to comfort, encourage, correct or summon them to action. Its purpose is spiritual commitment and growth. A difficult correction can therefore form part of exhortation, but repeated interactions that leave people unable to approach the speaker should prompt examination of the gift’s use.

questions.question: How can mercy be both a Christian responsibility and a particular gift?
questions.answer: Wesam affirms that all believers are called to be merciful. He also describes some people as especially able to share another person’s pain or joy in a way that refreshes and supports them. For him, the general command and distinctive giftedness belong together because the gifts express Christ’s character within the body.

questions.question: What helps distinguish service from a desire for attention or control?
questions.answer: Wesam asks whether people are being edified over time, rather than whether the speaker enjoys being admired. The discussion also commends giving honour to another person who can serve better. A desire for the spotlight is therefore an unreliable indicator of genuine gifted service.

questions.question: Is a church necessarily wrong when it does not give someone a public teaching role?
questions.answer: Wesam says the circumstances matter. Giftedness should be tested alongside character and faithful involvement, and teaching can begin in smaller settings rather than behind a pulpit. Deliberately blocking all appropriate service through control or favouritism is different. He also distinguishes selfish refusal to serve from lacking the capacity or opportunity to do so.

questions.question: How does church membership relate to the repeated call to serve one another?
questions.answer: Wesam understands the command as involving a defined group with mutual responsibilities. He therefore gives priority to service within the local church’s membership. He nevertheless allows helping believers elsewhere and receiving guest preachers, distinguishing those wider relationships from neglect of the immediate local responsibility.
